text: Compulsory question. Read the case study below and answer the questions. Ms. Neha Kulkarni, a 32‑year‑old HR executive, had been banking with Urban Trust Bank for almost a decade. She believed banks stood for stability and responsibility—qualities she valued deeply after witnessing her father struggle financially due to inadequate insurance coverage. On a rainy Monday morning, Neha walked into her familiar bank branch to prematurely close a fixed deposit to fund her sister’s wedding. As she waited, the atmosphere in the branch felt unusually tense. A senior relationship manager, Mr. Rohan Mehta, approached her with a warm smile and an urgent tone. He spoke about a “special protection plan” being offered in partnership with SecureLife Insurance Company, exclusively for long‑standing customers like her. He assured her that the policy was “safe, flexible, and fully endorsed by the bank.” Neha hesitated. She had always associated insurance with agents, not bank counters. Sensing her doubt, Rohan emphasized that purchasing insurance through the bank—bancassurance, as he called it—was more reliable than dealing with independent agents. He claimed the policy would secure her family’s future and required minimal paperwork, all of which could be handled instantly at the branch. Pressed for time and reassured by the bank’s reputation, Neha signed the documents. She was handed a welcome kit and told that all policy details would soon be emailed. As she stepped out into the drizzle, she felt a quiet relief—until days turned into weeks with no clear communication from the insurer. The suspense unfolded a month later when Neha finally read the policy document in detail. She realized that the policy had restrictions, exclusions, and premium commitments that were never clearly explained to her. The policy was not as flexible as suggested; surrender charges were high, and coverage benefits were conditional. Disturbed, Neha revisited the bank. This time, Rohan avoided eye contact. She was informed that the bank had merely acted as a corporate agent and responsibility now lay with the insurance company. Feeling misled, Neha questioned whether the convenience of bancassurance had overshadowed her right to informed consent. The incident left her torn between trust and caution. Was bancassurance truly a customer‑friendly innovation, or had convenience compromised transparency? Questions (6 Marks Each) 1. Analyze the limitation of bancassurance revealed through this situation. 2. Suggest measures to prevent issues such as those faced by Ms. Neha.

text: Compulsory question. Read the case study below and answer the questions. "RajanFinance — A Tale of Systemic Challenges in the Indian Financial System" Background: RajanFinance Ltd. is a mid-sized Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) registered with RBI, operating in Maharashtra. It mobilises short-term deposits from the public and lends to small businesses, housing, and agriculture. The company also invests surplus funds in money market instruments like Commercial Paper and Treasury Bills. In 2023, RajanFinance faced a severe liquidity crisis. Several of its large borrowers (real estate companies) defaulted, turning a significant portion of its loan book into Non- Performing Assets (NPAs). The company struggled to repay its depositors and was unable to roll over its short-term borrowings in the money market. Its credit rating was downgraded and it was unable to issue fresh Commercial Paper. Meanwhile, one of the company's directors secretly purchased put options (derivatives) on the company's shares before the NPA news was made public — a classic case of insider trading later investigated by SEBI. The company also had significant exposure to a crypto investment fund that had invested in various Virtual Digital Assets. The collapse of a major cryptocurrency wiped out a portion of this investment. RajanFinance had issued GDRs on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange three years earlier to raise foreign capital. As news of the crisis spread, GDR prices crashed, and Foreign Portfolio Investors pulled out their investments. The RBI intervened, directing the company to submit a resolution plan and consider merger with a scheduled commercial bank.
